cards.title: Prioritise CRO before driving traffic and use cost-per-lead math
cards.summary: Conversion rate optimization compounded against ad spend is the biggest lever in digital marketing; run the cost-per-lead math to justify doing it before buying traffic.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in site conversion work before or instead of increasing ad, SEO or social spend.
steps: Recognise that most marketing effort goes into acquisition (Google/Facebook ads, SEO, blogging, social) while almost nobody focuses on what happens after the click — and that post-click stage is usually the main area letting results down.

Diagnose the current baseline: many sites run at 0.5% or lower, meaning 200 visitors are needed for one lead or sale. Exposure Ninja reports regularly building sites in the 2%–10% range, sometimes higher.

Run the arithmetic against your own click costs. At £1 per click and a 1% conversion rate, 100 clicks (£100) buy one lead, so cost per lead is £100. Lifting conversion to 3% gives three leads per £100, i.e. £33 per lead.
Use that lower cost per lead to fund things the lower-converting site could not afford: higher ad bids, additional paid channels, or more traffic volume.
Sequence the work: run CRO first because every traffic channel you switch on costs money or time that a higher-converting site would use more efficiently.
caveats: The 2%–10% range is the presenter's agency claim, not an independent benchmark, and comes without methodology or sample detail.
The £1-click example is illustrative arithmetic, not a prediction for your account — substitute your real CPC and conversion data.

cards.title: Teach the conversion theory before touching the form
cards.summary: Implementation is trivial; without the psychological principles around the form it achieves nothing — so work the CLOSER framework from advert to sale first.
cards.use_when: Starting a CRO programme, or when a team keeps shipping button-colour and form-placement tweaks with disappointing results.
steps: Accept the framing: putting a button or form on a page is quick and easy, but unless you know what to write around that form and which psychological principles to apply on the rest of the page, the form is meaningless.
Stop treating CRO as 'move the form here' or 'change the button colour' — that is the trap that produces disappointment.
Aim for a clear conversion and sales process that starts at your advert and finishes with a client or a sale, rather than a set of isolated page tweaks.
Structure the work around the six CLOSER elements: credibility, lure, objection handling, social proof, ease, and delivering a result.
Work the theory stage first, then map implementation to your website platform — the precise build depends on the platform you are on.
Use real sites that execute each element well as reference examples while you work through credibility, lure and objections.
caveats: The six CLOSER elements are named here as an organising framework; detailed implementation for each is covered in the rest of the material rather than this overview.

cards.title: Give visitors a reason to believe you are good
cards.summary: Credibility is the first CLOSER element: if the site gives no reason to believe the business is good, visitors will not believe it and will not convert.
cards.use_when: Auditing a site that gets traffic but few enquiries, especially where the owner assumes a live website is itself proof of quality.
steps: State the principle plainly: if you do not give visitors a reason to believe what you do is good, they will not — and in fact cannot — believe it.
Recognise that your business is familiar to you but a stranger landing on your site sees just another website from another company in your category.

Test your own site honestly: put it on a screen and ask someone unfamiliar why they think the business is any good. If the answers are things like 'I like the logo', the site is doing a poor job of selling.
Inventory your credibility assets — testimonials, before/after stories, case-study statistics, client logos, awards and reviews, hyper-specific problem language, and background or story.
Place credibility on every page, and especially around the call to action, because that is the moment you are asking for trust. When asking someone to trust you, give them a reason to trust you.
Note the assets down before implementation so you can reuse them in CTAs, service pages and forms.
caveats: The source does not specify how to rank or weight credibility assets against each other.

cards.title: Use before-and-after storytelling as the core credibility format
cards.summary: Make the 'before' match where the audience is now and the 'after' match where they want to be, in pictures, testimonials, case studies or video.
cards.use_when: Building proof sections for a service or product site, or when testimonials read as vague praise that does not move anyone.
steps: Define the format's job: the before must resonate with the prospect's current situation ('that is me now') and the after must resonate with their desired outcome ('that is where I want to be').
Adapt the format to your business rather than copying fitness before/after photos — a testimonial, a case study, a webinar, or a results video all work if the before/after structure is intact.
Use the classic fitness example as the template: pictures paired with detailed written specifics, repeated many times down the page so the visitor sees the pattern.
Show variety across the examples — different ages and genders — so the impression is that this works for everyone, not just a narrow slice.
Match the emotional detail too: smiling after-photos and life-change details (one subject proposed to his long-term girlfriend) build a story around the person, not just the numbers.
Keep the structure consistent across every example so the page reads as a body of proof rather than isolated quotes.
caveats: Photographic before/afters translate directly to fitness-style results; the equivalent for B2B or services is testimonial, case-study or video format.

cards.title: Write meaningful specifics into testimonials, not vague praise
cards.summary: Precise, relatable details — 'fireman in California', '21 to 9% body fat' — build believability even when the details seem irrelevant to the result.
cards.use_when: Writing or rewriting testimonials, case studies and before/after copy that currently uses generic praise.
steps: Anchor each testimonial to a specific like age, job and location. 'At age 50' pre-empts the objection that it is too late; 'a fireman in California' tells readers he is a regular person, not a guru.
Accept that some specifics have no bearing on the result's quality — the fireman's job and state do not affect the camp's effectiveness, but they make the claim more believable and relatable.
Replace vague claims with exact figures: '21 to 9% body fat' and 'dropping 30 lbs on the scale', not 'lost loads of body fat'.
Close the loop explicitly: name the mechanism that produced the result (the 25-minute workouts, balanced nutrition, peer support community) so nobody has to guess that your offer caused it.
Include the person's job role and company when the proof is B2B — an events director seeing another events director endorse an AV company gets a direct before/after match.
Keep the wide-shots too: variety of ages and genders signals that the result is available to people like the reader.
caveats: The source notes even more specificity (e.g. 30.301 lbs) might be more believable but does not prescribe an optimal level of precision.
Do not fabricate specifics — these are real details extracted from real customers.

cards.title: Treat first impressions as judgments about your whole business
cards.summary: Visitors judge product quality, service, staff happiness and lead times from the site's look alone — and owners who built their own site cannot judge it objectively.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to reinvest in site design, or when you suspect aesthetics are suppressing enquiry rates.
steps: Run the seminar comparison as a diagnostic: show two sites from the same category, one polished and one basic, and ask which company has the better product, better customer service, happier employees, better reviews, shorter wait times. The polished one wins every question.

Accept the mechanism: until prospects have any other information about your business, the website's look and feel is all they have, so they extend that first impression to every aspect of the business.
Reject the 'do not judge a book by its cover' defence — as the presenter argues, that is exactly what covers are for.

Recognise that a redesigned site carries credibility for free: in the example, a roughly £4,000 website rebuild produced better perceptions of the product, service, staff and reviews without any operational change.
If your site looks like the weaker 'website A' example, treat it as an active problem, because people are judging you negatively.
Do not self-assess if you built the site — you are too close to it. Get an impartial review (the source suggests Exposure Ninja's free website and marketing review or a user-testing service) instead.
caveats: The comparison exercise is a seminar demonstration, not a measured study; no respondent counts, sampling or metrics are reported.
The 'evolutionarily programmed' justification for first-impression judgment is the presenter's assertion, not cited evidence.

cards.title: Put client logos and attributed testimonials above the fold
cards.summary: Move existing client logos, award badges and job-titled testimonials out of the About page and into the first screen and around CTAs.
cards.use_when: A site already has strong logos, awards or testimonials but visitors must dig for them.
steps: Audit what you already have: in the example, the company had worked with the NHS, BBC and others but the information was buried on an About page where nobody would find it.
Move client logos to the front and centre. Knowing that the BBC chose this supplier gives credibility because the BBC could choose anyone and made the same choice the prospect is contemplating.
Name the clients in the above-the-fold copy as well as showing logos — e.g. 'for over 11 years we have helped the likes of [client names]' — so the association is read, not just seen.
In every testimonial, include the person's job role as well as the company name, so a reader in the same role sees someone who was in their position and got the outcome they want.
Treat testimonials as before-and-after in text form: the peer's situation is the before, the result they describe ('the best AV company I have ever dealt with') is the after.
Also display awards won and Google reviews as an immediate credibility shortcut.
caveats: Client logos can normally only be used where permission or contractual terms allow — the source does not discuss permissions or usage rights.

cards.title: Spread case studies across service pages, not just the case studies page
cards.summary: Case-study pages are among the least-visited pages, so mirror matched case studies onto service pages and everywhere else — the logo alone carries the credibility.
cards.use_when: Populating service pages, or when case studies exist but sit only on a dedicated case studies URL.
steps: Keep the dedicated case studies page — it is worth having — but do not rely on it, because it tends to be one of the least visited pages on the site.
Place case studies on the service page for the specific service each one demonstrates, so relevance is obvious at the point of interest.
Show the client logo alongside each case study so the credibility works even for skimming visitors who never click through.
Accept that the full case study does not need to be read to deliver value: seeing the logo and knowing that business worked with you on that particular service is enough.
Push case-study proof out further still — the source says you really cannot overuse case studies and puts them on every page of the site.
Pair case studies with the client logos already placed above the fold for compounding effect.
caveats: Case studies need client consent for public use; the source does not cover permissions.
Effectiveness is asserted from practice, not reported with conversion data.

cards.title: Borrow credibility with hyper-niching when you have no testimonials
cards.summary: For new businesses, describing the prospect's problem so precisely that they feel understood builds immediate trust without case studies.
cards.use_when: You are new, have thin proof, and need a credibility route that does not rely on client history.
steps: Use what the source calls alternative credibility when testimonials and case studies are scarce.
Hyper-niche: choose a narrow audience and articulate their exact situation in your own copy rather than making general claims about your service.

Follow the accountancy example: instead of generic accounting copy, write to early-stage tech startups seeking investment — that you help them improve their numbers to secure investment, that you have worked with investors, and that you know what investors look for.
Aim for the palm-reader effect: when someone describes your situation so accurately that you think 'you really understand my situation', credibility arrives instantly without any testimonials.
Apply the same principle to your call-to-action wording so the CTA itself demonstrates that you understand the problem.
Keep the statement specific to a real segment you can actually serve — generic 'we help businesses grow' copy produces no recognition effect.
caveats: The source does not define how narrow the niche should be or how to phrase the problem statement.
Hyper-niching narrows the addressable audience; the source does not discuss the trade-off against broader reach.

cards.title: Use your own story and audience-relevant celebrity endorsement as credibility
cards.summary: Two further alternate credibility routes: background details that resonate with part of the audience, and endorsement from someone the audience already knows, likes and trusts.
cards.use_when: Newer or smaller businesses without heavy proof, looking for trust signals that do not depend on client logos.
steps: Mine your background for elements that overlap with your audience's identity, not a chronological life story. The presenter noticed that mentioning a past as a professional drummer made musicians and drummers approach him afterwards — the recognised detail created a bond ('you are just like me').
Select story elements by resonance, the same before/after test used elsewhere: does this detail place you where the audience is, or where they want to be?

For endorsements, do not buy generic celebrity fame. Choose someone who already has credibility with your specific audience — an industry figure, a publication figure, or a personality the audience has an existing relationship with, even if not technically famous.

Match the endorsement's presentation to that familiar context. In the Alan Titchmarsh life-insurance ad the subject stays in his gardening persona — informal shirt, mug in hand, as if he has just come in from the garden — because a suit would break the illusion and destroy the trust being borrowed.
Accept that the setting can be entirely irrelevant to the product (a garden has nothing to do with life insurance); what matters is keeping the familiar character intact.
caveats: The Titchmarsh example illustrates one execution of celebrity credibility; it is not a rule that every endorsement needs a specific prop, outfit or setting.
The drummer anecdote is a personal observation, not measured evidence of conversion impact.

cards.title: Design an attractive lure instead of a generic contact request
cards.summary: Replace 'Contact us' or 'Make an enquiry' with a concrete next step the visitor actually wants, because a bare enquiry request gives them no reason to act.
cards.use_when: Writing or auditing CTAs for a lead-generation site, or adapting the same process to e-commerce email capture.
steps: Check the current CTA's incentive: 'if they want to work with us they can make an enquiry' offers the visitor nothing — the only thing that happens is someone contacts them to sell. It is easier to ignore than to act on.
Recognise the fundamental mistake: sites are not converting because they are not incentivising anyone to become a lead.
Define the lure as the thing you give people to entice them to become a lead. On e-commerce the lure is usually the product itself; for services it must be designed deliberately.
Make the next step visible and tangible. The test: can you describe specifically how the lure moves the visitor closer to their goal? If you cannot, it is not compelling enough yet.

Do not create new giveaways before checking your existing sales process. Reframe steps you already perform — free consultations, calls, mockups, plans you already produce — and advertise the value in the CTA rather than adding cost.

Offer something in exchange for e-commerce email signups, such as a buyer guide, 10% off the first order, or free first-order postage. 'Subscribe to our newsletter' and 'enquire' carry no perceived value because they advance the seller's journey, not the visitor's.
caveats: The source asserts newsletter signups have zero perceived value without supporting data and does not say whether any newsletter offer could ever work.

cards.title: Learn from lure examples and their reported conversion spread
cards.summary: Positioning a weak lure gives 0–1%; a strong, well-positioned lure with a concrete outcome has been reported at 10–15% (up to 30% on some channels).
cards.use_when: Benchmarking what a CTA change might be worth, or diagnosing why a form that is present still converts poorly.
steps: Compare the solicitor example: the enquiry form sits above the fold (good positioning, worth roughly 2–3% on positioning alone) but the copy is 'How can we help? Make an inquiry' with no lure at all — so there is no reason to bother.

Compare the construction example: the copy 'request a quote' is a reasonable lure seed, but it is stuck at the bottom of the page and the form is not even shown, so a site like this typically converts between zero and 1%.

Contrast with the PPI example, where the CTA reframes the enquiry as a concrete deliverable: 'We find out if you had PPI' rather than 'inquire with us'. That page is reported at 10–15%, reaching 30% on some channels, versus a stated average around 0.5%–1%.
Note the reported volume context: at peak the PPI site received roughly 400 leads a day, and 200 leads in an hour after a TV programme sent people searching for PPI companies.
Test sharper wording: a variant reading 'Find out how much you could claim' (rather than 'if') was reported at 33.7% across the whole site, though the picture and headline changed at the same time.
Treat the spread as directional: the same form can be no-lure-and-buried, lure-but-buried, or lure-and-prominent, and the conversion range follows.
caveats: No sample sizes, time periods, traffic sources or measurement methods are given for any of these figures.
The 33.7% result bundles wording with picture and headline changes, so the wording's isolated contribution is unknown.
The stated comparator average is ambiguous as transcribed, and the 30% channel is described only as 'in this case organic traffic'.

cards.title: Do not push visitors further down the buyer journey than they are
cards.summary: The ADT split test: matching the CTA to what the audience already wants — a price — beat a higher-perceived-value offer by 60%.
cards.use_when: Choosing CTA wording when your audience has already decided they want the category and just need the practical next detail.
steps: Review the test: 'Book a free survey' versus 'Get a free quote', identical except for wording. 'Get a free quote' produced a reported 60% uplift.

Analyse the perceived cost of each option. 'Book a free survey' implies someone comes to your house, probably a salesperson, and you will be sold to — friction and risk. 'Get a free quote' could be a form and an email with no conversation at all.
Account for the audience's starting position: ADT's customers already knew they were interested and already knew they wanted the thing. All they wanted was a price so they could decide or disqualify.
Do not over-engineer the first step. Taking a step too far down the buyer journey (a booked appointment) added perceived pain that outweighed the survey's higher perceived value.
Apply the general principle: if the offering is simple, keep it simple. Match the CTA to the step the visitor is ready to take.
Add the diagnostic question when designing any CTA: what is the perceived pain and risk of saying yes to this, versus the perceived value of the thing offered?
caveats: No sample size, test duration, statistical significance or metric definition (conversion rate versus lead volume) is reported for the 60% uplift.
The source does not explain how to determine that an audience has already established its need; that judgement must come from your own research.

cards.title: Match the lure to whether the audience knows the scale of its problem
cards.summary: If prospects cannot size their problem, the lure should help them see it; if they can, the lure should hand them a plan — examples span marketing reviews, 3D mockups and funding plans.
cards.use_when: Choosing what to offer in exchange for an enquiry when you are unsure how aware your audience is.
steps: Rule 1: if the audience does not know the scale of their problem, the conversion process helps them figure it out. Get them to a stage where they understand what their problem looks like and can visualise a future.

Exposure Ninja's marketing review applies this: it identifies what competitors are doing, shows the holes in the prospect's own digital marketing, and shows what is possible — a deliverable that quantifies an unclear problem.
Cosmetic surgery and architecture fit the same rule: a free consultation plus a mockup or initial visual so the prospect can see the result and the scale of what they would get.
An exhibition-stand client changed its CTA from 'get a quote' to a free no-obligation consultation about the stand plus a free 3D visual mockup — the mockup lets the buyer picture the outcome.

Rule 2: if the audience already knows the scale of its problem, give them a road map. A funding client's CTA is a free consultation covering funding options plus a plan for successfully funding the business.

For prospects who already know what they want (e.g. 'we need PPC management and want to cut cost per acquisition'), analyse their current campaign and set out the things you would work on — proving competence and showing the route to the goal.
Whatever the route, the offer must yield a visible tangible next-step picture, not an abstract promise.
caveats: The source gives no method for assessing which state your audience is in — that must come from your own audience research.
No conversion results are reported for the marketing review, funding, cosmetic surgery or exhibition-stand examples.

cards.title: Answer first-step objections before asking anyone to convert
cards.summary: Beyond sales objections about price or product, websites must defuse inertia to act — the fear, doubt and uncertainty that stop a first action entirely.
cards.use_when: Reworking a form or CTA that gets traffic but no submissions, especially for local or geographically limited services.
steps: Separate the two objection types: objections raised later in the sales process (price too high, delivery too slow) versus the first-step objection — inertia to act.
Accept the mechanic: unless a certain number of red flags are answered, visitors will not attempt to contact you, enquire, buy a first purchase or sign up at all.

Model it as a balance: the visitor has the goal your product delivers on one side and fear, doubt and uncertainty weighing against the decision on the other. Which of the three dominates depends on what you sell.

Audit a real page for unanswered first-step questions. In the construction example, 'request a free quote' left prospects wondering: do you even serve my area, when the site shows only central London and Ealing? Getting that wrong risks embarrassment or a wasted call.

Answer the second common objection — what happens after I submit? The page gave no indication whether a salesperson calls, someone visits the house, or they are invited into an office. Many prospects cannot accommodate that.

Recognise who actually submits an unexplained form: the very gung-ho, or people who already know they want to buy. The latter need no optimisation at all — they just need a form. The people worth designing for are the ones on the edge, undecided between you and a competitor.
Place the answers directly on the page and near the form so the red flags are cleared before the decision point.
caveats: The source does not provide a complete list of first-step objections; the construction example illustrates the method rather than enumerating every case.
Objection content is audience-specific — verify against your own prospects rather than copying the examples.

cards.title: Instrument phone, chat and form conversions so lead behaviour is measurable
cards.summary: Add call tracking, live chat, callback widgets and landing-page tooling so phone leads and diverse behaviours are attributed and counted.
cards.use_when: Setting up the measurement layer for conversion work, particularly for service businesses that receive phone leads.
steps: Add dynamic call tracking so phone leads attribute back to the specific ad campaign and keyword that produced them — this is the role the source assigns to Response Tap.
Add live chat for on-site conversations and lead capture (Tawk.to is named as the example).
Add callback widgets so visitors can request a call rather than being forced to dial (Live Call is named).
Consider landing-page tooling for building and testing the entry pages that feed the process — Leadpages is named in the source's tool list.
Plan ahead for how multiple lead types (calls, chats, callbacks, form submissions) will be counted together, since the point of the tooling is capturing and measuring diverse lead behaviours.
Match the specific implementation to your website platform; the source notes precise implementation depends on what your site runs on, while the tools themselves can be applied regardless.
caveats: The source does not give configuration steps, selection criteria or measurement definitions for these tools, and only names them in passing.
Tool interfaces and features change — verify current capabilities and setup directly before relying on them.
The source explicitly skips general UI walkthroughs for tools such as Tawk.to and Leadpages.
